questions.question: Name the four factors of production and their remuneration, and explain, using one characteristic of each factor, why that factor is paid the way it is.
questions.expected_answer: Natural resources earn rent, labour earns wages and salaries, capital earns interest, and entrepreneurship earns profit. Natural resources are fixed in total supply and cannot be produced, so quantity supplied cannot expand when price rises and rent is determined almost entirely by demand — a well-placed shop site is expensive because nobody can manufacture another one. Labour is inseparable from the worker and perishable, so it is hired as an ongoing service at a negotiated wage rather than bought outright, with unions, bargaining councils, the national minimum wage and productivity shaping the figure. Capital is produced by saving and investment and it depreciates, so its reward is interest, the price of the funds that acquired it. Entrepreneurship carries the uninsurable risk and is paid last, which makes profit a residual that can be negative — and that is precisely why the entrepreneur is the one who decides.

questions.question: A Gqeberha firm sells R4 000 000 of output and buys in R1 500 000 of steel, electricity and services. It pays wages of R1 600 000, rent of R240 000 and interest of R160 000, and sets aside R200 000 for consumption of fixed capital. Calculate value added and profit, and explain why the bought-in items are excluded.
questions.expected_answer: Value added is the value of output minus intermediate purchases: R4 000 000 minus R1 500 000 gives R2 500 000. Wages, rent, interest and depreciation together come to R2 200 000, so profit as the residual is R2 500 000 minus R2 200 000, which is R300 000. Adding all five components back returns exactly R2 500 000, which is the check. The R1 500 000 of steel, electricity and services is intermediate consumption, not a factor payment: those inputs already generated wages, rent, interest and profit inside the firms that supplied them, so counting them again in this firm's value added would count the same income twice. Note also that consumption of fixed capital is not income to anyone — it is capital used up and set aside for replacement — so net value added is R2 300 000.

questions.question: Explain how local economic planning, accessibility for marginalised groups, community participation and empowerment procurement work together to widen access to the factors of production in South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Local economic planning starts from the municipality's constitutional duty to promote development: every municipality adopts and annually reviews an Integrated Development Plan, and its economic core is a factor question — which resources, skills and infrastructure does this place have, and how can they be combined here rather than exported raw? Accessibility asks who is currently blocked from those factors, and the barriers must be named precisely: no registered title means no collateral and therefore no loan; no information means tenders pass by unseen; apartheid settlement patterns put households far from work so a large share of a low income goes on transport; and supply contracts flow along existing networks. Community participation through ward committees and IDP forums lowers the cost of a good decision because local knowledge reveals which needs bind hardest, and projects a community helped choose are maintained. Empowerment procurement then supplies the demand: B-BBEE scores a firm on ownership, management control, skills development, enterprise and supplier development and socio-economic development, and the Preferential Procurement Policy Framework Act's 80/20 and 90/10 points systems award most points for price and a fixed remainder for transformation goals. Because the state is the largest single buyer in the economy, redirecting part of its spending redirects demand — and demand is what turns idle factors into factor incomes.
